title: Motion Planning As Reduction
notes: Open by naming the chapter's main move: a robot moving through continuous space becomes a smaller geometric object that can be searched. The deck follows the printed span 294-346, with provenance that these pages map to PDF pages 303-355. Emphasize that every visual today is synthetic or notebook-generated, not a textbook figure.

title: The Planning Problem
notes: Set up the vocabulary before any algorithm appears. A configuration is one complete placement of the robot, obstacles carve out forbidden configurations, and a feasible motion is a continuous curve that stays in free space. The drawing deliberately separates workspace intuition from configuration-space bookkeeping.

title: Three Questions: Decision, Path, Shortest
notes: Frame the chapter as a hierarchy of tasks, not a single problem. The decision question asks only whether two configurations lie in the same free-space component. The path question asks for a witness curve. The shortest-path question adds an optimization layer, which is why visibility graphs and Dijkstra enter.

title: Point Robot: Infinite Paths To Finite Graph
notes: Use the notebook visual as the first concrete reduction. Infinitely many polygonal routes are possible, but a shortest route only needs to turn at obstacle vertices. Once those visible vertex pairs are turned into graph edges, the geometric problem becomes a weighted graph problem with fourteen nodes and twenty-seven visibility edges in the checked scene.

title: Visibility Lemma Proof Roadmap
notes: The proof idea should feel physical. If a shortest path bends in empty space, slide or pull the bend until it either disappears or hits an obstacle vertex. Repeating this local straightening leaves only start, target, and obstacle vertices as possible turn points. That is the bridge from continuous paths to a finite graph.

title: Dijkstra As Paint Spread
notes: Explain Dijkstra with the paint-spread picture because it matches shortest-path geometry. Distances expand from the start like a front. The next settled vertex is the first unsettled vertex reached by the front, so its distance can no longer improve. In the notebook scene, the settled chain recovers s, O0.1, O1.1, and t.

title: Disk Robot: Grow The Obstacles
notes: Now change the robot, not the algorithm. A disk collides when its center gets within one radius of an obstacle, so the disk center must avoid expanded obstacles. This converts the disk robot back into a point robot problem, provided the start and target centers remain outside the grown forbidden regions.

title: Minkowski Sum Language
notes: Introduce Minkowski addition as the notation that makes obstacle growth precise. The forbidden reference-point region is the obstacle plus the reflected robot. Reflection matters because we ask where the robot's reference point can be placed so that some robot point overlaps an obstacle point.

title: Convex Polygon Translation
notes: Use the convex robot artifact to make the formula computational. The notebook forms all pairwise sums between obstacle vertices and reflected robot vertices, then takes the convex hull. In the checked example, fifteen pairwise sums collapse to an eight-vertex convex configuration-space obstacle.

title: From Translation To Free-Space Components
notes: Tie the growth construction to the decision problem. Once every obstacle is replaced by a configuration-space obstacle, the question is whether the start and target reference points occupy the same connected component of free space. A path planner can then search a roadmap, a cell graph, or another finite representation.

title: Ladder: Rotation Adds A Dimension
notes: The ladder is the warning that translation-only pictures are not enough. A rigid segment has position and angle, so the configuration space has one more dimension than the floor plan. Narrow passages can be reachable only by coordinating translation with rotation, which is why the slide uses slices by angle.

title: Cell Decomposition And Retraction
notes: Present cell decomposition as the general recipe behind many planners. Decompose free space into simple cells, connect adjacent cells in a graph, and retract each cell to a lower-dimensional spine. The important idea is not the exact decomposition shown, but the reduction from continuous motion to graph connectivity.

title: Robot Arm Reachability Annulus
notes: Switch from translating bodies to an articulated chain. The endpoint cannot go farther than the sum of link lengths, and if one link dominates all the others it also cannot get too close to the base. The checked notebook instance has outer radius 4.1, inner radius 0, and the target lies inside that annulus.

title: Two-Kinks Construction
notes: The two-kinks theorem compresses many joint angles into two grouped directions. Partition the links into two straight subchains, solve the two-circle intersection problem for the grouped lengths, then unfold each group along the same direction. The notebook witness uses grouped lengths 2.6 and 1.5 and reaches the target to numerical precision.

title: Separability: Easy Order, Hard Variants
notes: The separability section changes the flavor of the chapter. For convex pieces translating in one fixed direction, a clean order can remove one piece at a time. But general variants can encode combinatorial choices, including Partition-style and Towers-of-Hanoi-style behavior, so the easy ordering theorem should not be mistaken for a universal planner.

title: Reduction Map Recap
notes: Close by revisiting the chapter goal: each motion-planning family becomes a geometric reduction, and then often a graph or ordering problem. Point robots use visibility graphs, disks use offset obstacles, convex translators use Minkowski sums, ladders use configuration-space dimensions, arms use annuli and circle intersections, and separability exposes both clean orders and hard variants.
